description:
What If You Watched a Moon Fall Out of the Sky?

Episode 98 of a daily journey through the universe. 🌑
We orbit Phobos, the bigger moon of Mars: a 22 km potato that circles Mars three times a day, rises in the west, is spiraling inward about 2 meters every century, and will be torn apart or crash in about 30 to 50 million years.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 99: Next stop, Vesta. A giant asteroid with a mountain twice as tall as Everest.

Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

segments.text: One of Mars's moons is falling, and one day it will crash or shatter.
Mars has two tiny moons. The bigger one is Phobos, a lumpy rock only about twenty-two kilometers across.
It orbits just six thousand kilometers above the surface of Mars. Closer than any other moon to its planet.
segments.headline: Very close to Mars

segments.text: It's so fast that it circles Mars three times a day. From the ground, it rises in the west and sets in the east.
One giant crater, Stickney, is almost half as wide as the whole moon. The impact nearly shattered it.
segments.headline: Stickney crater

segments.text: But here's the twist. Mars's gravity is slowly pulling Phobos inward, about two meters every century.
segments.headline: It's falling

segments.text: Those long grooves on its surface may be stretch marks, as Mars tugs on it.
segments.headline: Stretch marks?

segments.text: In about thirty to fifty million years, Phobos will crash into Mars, or be torn apart into a ring.

visual.label: years left
visual.sub: then a crash, or a ring

segments.text: Japan's MMX mission plans to land on Phobos and bring a piece of it back to Earth.
segments.headline: A sample is coming

segments.text: Tomorrow, we fly to the asteroid belt, to a giant asteroid with a mountain more than twice as tall as Everest. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
